props.title: Walker

sections.content: Walker stands as one of Alex Cox's most audacious and politically charged films, deliberately mixing 19th century historical drama with jarring modern anachronisms. Ed Harris plays William Walker, the American mercenary who briefly ruled Nicaragua in the 1850s, with an intensity that mirrors the film's savage critique of U.S. imperialism. Cox's punk sensibility meshes perfectly with the material, using Coca-Cola cans, modern magazines, and helicopters to connect 1850s American interventionism directly to 1980s Reagan-era foreign policy in Central America. The film pairs naturally with other politically radical 80s films like Salvador (1986) and Missing (1982). Salvador|1986|James Woods plays a cynical photojournalist documenting US-backed violence in El Salvador. Oliver Stone's brutal critique of American foreign policy.|Prime Missing|1982|Jack Lemmon searches for his missing son in Chile during Pinochet's coup. Costa-Gavras masterfully blends thriller elements with political commentary.|Criterion Burn!|1969|Marlon Brando plays a British agent manipulating a Caribbean island's revolution. Brilliant critique of colonialism.|Tubi

Cox's anarchic style in Walker draws from a tradition of politically radical filmmaking that includes Gillo Pontecorvo's The Battle of Algiers (1966) and Francesco Rosi's Salvatore Giuliano (1962). These films share a commitment to exposing colonial violence while experimenting with form and chronology. Cox pushes this further by completely shattering historical authenticity, using anachronism as a weapon to connect past and present imperialism. The film's commercial failure and savage reviews led to Cox being essentially blacklisted from Hollywood, making it a fascinating example of how political filmmaking can derail a promising mainstream career.

The film's influence can be seen in later works that mix historical drama with contemporary elements, like Ravenous (1999) and The Good Lord Bird (2020). Joe Strummer's score perfectly captures the film's punk sensibility, creating a sonic bridge between periods that matches Cox's visual strategy. The violence is particularly shocking, deliberately echoing news footage from Nicaragua and El Salvador that would have been familiar to 1987 audiences. The Battle of Algiers|1966|Revolutionary classic about Algeria's fight for independence. Documentary-style realism meets political passion.|Criterion Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid|1973|Sam Peckinpah deconstructs Western myths with contemporary resonance. Bob Dylan score adds temporal complexity.|HBO Max SUBHEAD: Political Cinema and Historical Revisionism

Walker belongs to a vital tradition of American films that critique U.S. imperialism through genre subversion, including Apocalypse Now (1979) and The Deer Hunter (1978). What sets Cox's film apart is its total commitment to anachronistic elements as political commentary. The film's finale, with modern helicopters evacuating Americans while Nicaragua burns, creates a devastating parallel between Walker's time and 1980s Central American intervention. This technique would influence later films like Sorry to Bother You (2018) and The Last Black Man in San Francisco (2019) in their use of surreal elements to address political realities.
